results.summary_before: This project is a 7-segment display counter that increments once per second, counting up to 10. It uses a clock divider and combinational logic to convert binary to decimal for the display, with the bottom 8 bits of the counter also output on the bidirectional pins. The counting speed can be adjusted by setting the input pins to override bits 11-18 of a 24-bit compare register; with all inputs zero, the compare is 10,000,000, giving a 1-second interval at 10 MHz. The design requires a 10 MHz clock and a 7-segment display; no silicon test results are provided.

results.summary_before: This Wokwi design is a multi-channel pulse counter with serial output, counting pulses on four input channels within a time interval measured by an RTC. It includes four 12-bit counters, overflow detection, and a state machine that periodically reads out the RTC time and counter values serially. Testing involves applying short pulses to the input channels and clocking out the serial data when overflow is signaled; the design is an early work-in-progress for a low-power sensor interface for acoustic emission detection. It is notable for its application in sensor interfaces and non-destructive testing, though the documentation notes it is a work in progress.

Silicon testing confirmed that the generator works as described when following the author's instructions.

results.summary_before: This design is a configurable pseudo-random binary sequence generator built around a Galois LFSR with XOR taps, supporting polynomial sizes up to 16 bits. It is configured over an SPI mode 0 interface with four registers controlling command/address, clock divider, polynomial enable bits, and tap selection. Outputs include differential PRBS and look-ahead versions of the next bit, and a fail-safe all-zeros check prevents lock-up. It requires an external SPI controller, a clock input, and a logic analyzer to observe the generated sequence.
